title: Data Wrangling with pandas and NumPy
subtitle: Turn messy, scattered data into clean, analysis-ready tables: vectorised NumPy, pandas' index and dtypes, missing data, validated merges, reshaping and group operations.
outcomes: Process arrays with vectorised NumPy operations, broadcasting and masks, and tell views from copies
Build, load and index Series and DataFrames, using alignment and Copy-on-Write to your advantage
Find and handle missing data, sentinels, duplicates and impossible values, and document every decision
Merge, join and concatenate datasets with validated keys, and reshape between long and wide forms
Summarise data with groupby, named aggregation, transform, filter, pivot tables and crosstabs
prerequisites: Python Foundations for Data Science, or the same Python: functions, loops, dictionaries and comprehensions. Data Analysis with Python and pandas helps but isn't required: this course goes further into NumPy, pandas' index and types, messy cleaning, validated merges, reshaping and group operations. You need Python 3 with NumPy and pandas 2.2 or later (pandas 3 differences are noted), and JupyterLab if you like notebooks. Every dataset comes with the labs.
description:
Real data rarely arrives ready to analyse. It comes in several files that don't quite agree, with gaps, codes typed three ways, values in the wrong units and rows that repeat. Data wrangling is the work of turning it into one clean, trustworthy table, and this course teaches it with the two libraries that do it in Python: NumPy and pandas. You'll start beneath pandas, with NumPy's arrays: computing a vegetation index for every pixel of a satellite tile at once, masking clouds, and using broadcasting, reshaping and views. Then you'll learn how pandas' Series and DataFrames really work: the index and the alignment it brings, read_csv options for awkward files, dtypes that save memory and keep data honest, and how Copy-on-Write in pandas 3 changes the way you modify data.

The heart of the course is messy data. You'll clean a reef monitoring export with missing-value markers, sentinels, duplicates and impossible values, combine livestock censuses with district data and satellite passes using merges you validate and audit, reshape between long and wide, and summarise two years of rangeland monitoring with groupby, transform, pivot tables and crosstabs. Every lab's data is made up for the course and comes with it, and every lab prints results you can check exactly. The capstone brings it all together: two overlapping exports from an air-quality network, cleaned, merged with station and weather data, gap-filled and summarised into an analysis-ready dataset, with a cleaning log and checks that would catch each problem if it returned.

modules.title: Introduction to NumPy
modules.summary: Work with NumPy's n-dimensional arrays: how they store data, vectorised operations and universal functions, broadcasting between shapes, and indexing that gives views or copies, on a satellite image.

lessons.title: The ndarray: shape, dtype and memory
objectives: Create arrays and read their shape, dtype and size
Explain why arrays are faster and more compact than lists of numbers
key_points: A NumPy ndarray is a grid of values of one type, its dtype, stored in one contiguous block of memory, so operations run in compiled code without checking each element's type the way Python does for a list.

shape gives the size of each dimension, ndim the number of dimensions, size the number of elements and nbytes the memory used: a 20 x 20 array of float64 has shape (20, 20), size 400 and takes 3,200 bytes.

np.array() makes an array from a list; np.zeros, np.ones and np.full fill a shape with one value, np.arange(start, stop, step) counts like range, np.linspace(a, b, n) gives n evenly spaced values and np.loadtxt reads a text file of numbers.

One dtype covers the whole array: mixing ints and floats gives float64, and astype() converts by making a new array. float32 halves the memory at the cost of precision, and fixed-size integers wrap around silently when they overflow: an int8 of 127 plus 1 is -128.

For random numbers, make a generator with rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) and call its methods, such as rng.normal() or rng.integers(); the same seed gives the same numbers, so results can be reproduced.

lessons.title: Vectorised operations and universal functions
objectives: Replace loops with whole-array arithmetic, ufuncs and aggregations
Aggregate along an axis and handle missing values with NaN-aware functions
key_points: Arithmetic on arrays works element by element: (nir - red) / (nir + red) computes a vegetation index for every pixel at once. This is vectorisation: the loop runs in compiled code, which is usually many times faster than a Python loop over the same values.
Universal functions (ufuncs) such as np.sqrt, np.exp, np.log and np.abs apply element by element, and comparisons such as ndvi > 0.5 give a boolean array of the same shape.
Aggregations take an axis: on a 2-D array, a.sum(axis=0) collapses the rows, giving one total per column, a.mean(axis=1) gives one mean per row, and no axis aggregates every element.
np.where(condition, x, y) chooses values element by element, np.select picks between several conditions, np.digitize bins values, and the mean of a boolean array is the share of True values.

NaN marks a missing float and spreads through arithmetic: np.mean returns nan if any value is nan, while np.nanmean, np.nansum and np.nanmax skip them. Any comparison with NaN is False, so test with np.isnan.
Dividing by zero gives inf or nan with a RuntimeWarning; np.divide(a, b, out=np.full(a.shape, np.nan), where=b != 0) divides only where it's safe and leaves NaN elsewhere.

Time the loop, then the vectorised expression.
steps.see: The vectorised line is far faster; the exact times depend on your computer.

lessons.title: Broadcasting: arrays of different shapes
objectives: Predict the result's shape when NumPy combines arrays of different shapes
Use keepdims and np.newaxis to line up dimensions
key_points: Broadcasting lets an operation combine arrays of different shapes without copying data: a scalar combines with any array, and a (20,) array of column means can be subtracted from a (20, 20) array.

The rule: compare the shapes from the last dimension backwards. Two dimensions fit when they're equal or one of them is 1, and a missing leading dimension counts as 1; the result takes the larger size of each.
A (20, 20) array minus a (20,) array lines up with the columns, so per-row values need a column shape: a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) has shape (20, 1), and so does a.mean(axis=1)[:, np.newaxis].
Shapes that don't fit raise an error such as operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (20,20) (5,), which is far better than a silently wrong result.
Standardising every column is one line: (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0) broadcasts two (n_columns,) arrays over an (n_rows, n_columns) table.
Outer operations broadcast too: a[:, np.newaxis] * b gives the product of every item of a with every item of b, as a grid of shape (len(a), len(b)).

lessons.title: Indexing, slicing, views and copies
objectives: Select with slices, integer arrays and boolean masks
Tell when a selection is a view that shares memory with the original
key_points: a[i, j] picks one element of a 2-D array, a[2:5, :] rows 2 to 4 and a[:, -1] the last column; slices follow Python's rules, so the stop index is left out.

Basic slicing returns a view, a new array object that shares the original's memory, so changing the view changes the original. np.shares_memory(a, b) tells you whether two arrays overlap, and .copy() makes an independent array.
Fancy indexing with integer arrays, such as a[[0, 3, 7]], and boolean masks, such as a[a > 0.5], always return copies.
Assigning through a mask changes the original in place: ndvi[cloud] = np.nan blanks every cloudy pixel.
reshape() returns a view whenever it can and keeps the elements in order: a 20 x 20 grid reshaped to (4, 5, 4, 5) and averaged over axes 1 and 3 gives a 4 x 4 grid of 5 x 5 block means.
Python list slices are copies but NumPy slices are views, so code written for lists can behave differently when it meets arrays; ravel() may return a view, while flatten() always copies.

files.content:
"""Process one 20 x 20 tile of a satellite image with NumPy (made-up data).

red.csv and nir.csv hold the reflectance of each pixel in the red and near-infrared bands, from 0 to 1.
Fill in the TODOs, then run:  python ndvi_tile.py
"""

import numpy as np

red = np.loadtxt("red.csv", delimiter=",")
nir = np.loadtxt("nir.csv", delimiter=",")

# 1. What did we load?
print("Shape:", red.shape, "dtype:", red.dtype, "size:", red.size, "bytes:", red.nbytes)

# 2. The vegetation index NDVI = (nir - red) / (nir + red), for every pixel at once, without a loop.
# Pixels where nir + red is 0 have no data: leave them as NaN instead of dividing by zero.
# TODO: use np.divide with out= and where=
ndvi = np.full(red.shape, np.nan)
print("No-data pixels:", int(np.isnan(ndvi).sum()))

# 3. Clouds are bright in the red band: treat every pixel with red > 0.25 as cloud and blank it.
# TODO: a boolean mask, then assignment through it
cloud = np.zeros(red.shape, dtype=bool)
print("Cloud pixels:", int(cloud.sum()))
valid = np.isfinite(ndvi)
print("Valid pixels:", int(valid.sum()))

# 4. Summaries that ignore the NaN pixels
# TODO: replace the zeros with np.nanmean, np.nanmax and the share of valid pixels above 0.5
mean_ndvi, max_ndvi, dense_share = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
print(f"Mean NDVI: {mean_ndvi:.3f}, max: {max_ndvi:.3f}")
print(f"Share of valid pixels above 0.5: {dense_share:.1%}")

# 5. Classes: water below 0, bare 0 to 0.2, sparse 0.2 to 0.5, dense from 0.5
# TODO: np.digitize the valid values with the bins [0, 0.2, 0.5], then count each class with np.bincount
counts = np.zeros(4, dtype=int)
print("Classes:", dict(zip(["water", "bare", "sparse", "dense"], counts.tolist())))

# 6. Broadcasting: anomalies from each column's mean, and from each row's mean
# TODO: column means have shape (20,); row means need keepdims=True to have shape (20, 1)
col_means = row_means = np.zeros(1)
print("Column means:", col_means.shape, "row means:", row_means.shape)
print("Anomaly shapes:", (ndvi - col_means).shape, (ndvi - row_means).shape)
try:
    ndvi - np.ones(5)
except ValueError as err:
    print("Error:", err)

# 7. Block averages: the mean of each 5 x 5 block, as a 4 x 4 grid, with reshape and one call
# TODO: reshape to (4, 5, 4, 5) and take np.nanmean over axes 1 and 3
blocks = np.zeros((4, 4))
print("Block means:")
print(np.round(blocks, 2))

# 8. Views and copies
corner = ndvi[:5, :5]
print("Slice shares memory:", np.shares_memory(corner, ndvi))
print("Mask selection shares memory:", np.shares_memory(ndvi[valid], ndvi))
tile = ndvi.copy()
view = tile[:2, :2]
view[:] = 0
# TODO: what does changing the view do to tile? Print tile[0, 0] and explain it in a comment.

hints: np.divide divides only where where= is True; out= supplies the value (NaN here) for every other pixel.
Take the share over ndvi[valid], not the whole tile, or the NaN pixels count as False and lower it.
reshape(4, 5, 4, 5) splits each axis of 20 into 4 blocks of 5; axes 1 and 3 are the positions inside a block.

modules.title: Pandas Data Structures
modules.summary: Understand pandas' Series and DataFrame: values with an index, the alignment the index brings, building and loading tables from dictionaries and messy files, and selecting data safely under Copy-on-Write.

lessons.title: Series: values with an index
objectives: Create a Series and select from it by label and by position
Explain how a Series relates to a NumPy array
key_points: A Series is a one-dimensional array of values with an index of labels, a dtype and an optional name: pd.Series({'S01': 4.5, 'S02': 12.0}, name='depth_m') takes its labels from the dictionary's keys.
Underneath is an array: s.to_numpy() returns it, and vectorised arithmetic and NumPy functions work on a Series while keeping its index.

s.loc['S02'] selects by label and s.iloc[0] by position. Be explicit: in pandas 3, s[0] always means the label 0 and raises KeyError if there's no such label, whereas older versions fell back to the position with a warning.
A boolean mask filters a Series as it filters an array, as in s[s > 10], and methods such as sort_values(), value_counts() and describe() return new objects.
pandas marks missing values as NaN, or as <NA> in its nullable types; s.isna() finds them, and sum(), mean() and most other methods skip them by default.

lessons.title: The index: alignment and fast look-ups
objectives: Predict the result of arithmetic between objects with different indexes
Set, reset and use an index, including a MultiIndex
key_points: Operations between two Series line up their labels first: adding two divers' counts per genus matches the genera by name, whatever their order, and a label found in only one Series gives NaN.
Methods such as s1.add(s2, fill_value=0) treat a label missing from one side as 0, which suits counts; for measurements, NaN is usually the honest answer.

set_index('site_id') moves a column into the index and reset_index() moves it back; sort_index() sorts by label, and reindex(labels) conforms an object to a given list of labels, adding NaN for new ones.
A unique index makes label look-ups fast, like a dictionary's keys. Check index.is_unique, because a repeated label makes .loc return several rows where you expected one.
A MultiIndex has several levels, such as (site_id, date): df.loc['S03'] selects every row for one site, and df.loc[('S03', '2024-03-04')] a single row.

lessons.title: DataFrames: build, load and inspect
objectives: Build DataFrames from dictionaries, records and arrays
Load a messy text file with the right read_csv options and dtypes
key_points: A DataFrame is a table of columns, each a Series, sharing one row index: pd.DataFrame from a dictionary of lists makes a column per key, and from a list of dictionaries a row per dictionary.

read_csv adapts to the file: sep=';' for semicolons, decimal=',' for decimal commas, comment='#' to skip notes, na_values=['n/a', '-'] for missing markers, usecols to read some columns and nrows for a quick look.

Set types on purpose: dtype={'island': 'category'} stores repeated labels as small codes, the nullable 'Int64' keeps whole numbers whole when some are missing, and pd.to_datetime(col, format='%d.%m.%Y') parses dates exactly.
info() lists each column's dtype and non-missing count, and memory_usage(deep=True) the bytes each uses; text columns show as str in pandas 3 and as object in earlier versions.
shape, columns, index and dtypes describe a table; head(), sample(5, random_state=0) and describe(include='all') give a first look at its values.

lessons.title: Selecting data safely: loc, iloc and Copy-on-Write
objectives: Select rows and columns by label, position and condition
Change values in one step, without chained assignment
key_points: df.loc[rows, cols] selects by label or condition, and a label slice such as 'S01':'S03' includes both ends; df.iloc[rows, cols] selects by position, and its slices leave out the end, as in Python.
df.at[label, column] and df.iat[i, j] read or set a single value quickly.

Copy-on-Write is the default in pandas 3 and can be switched on in pandas 2: every selection behaves as a copy, so changing it never changes the original, and data is copied only when one of them is modified.

Chained assignment, such as df[df['coral_pct'] > 100]['coral_pct'] = None, changes nothing under Copy-on-Write, and pandas warns about it. Write it as one step: df.loc[df['coral_pct'] > 100, 'coral_pct'] = None.
Take a subset you mean to change with .copy(): it states the intent and avoids the SettingWithCopyWarning that pandas 2 can show.
where() keeps the values where a condition holds and replaces the rest, with NaN by default, and mask() does the opposite: df['coral_pct'].mask(df['coral_pct'] > 100) blanks the impossible values.

files.content:
"""Build, align and load reef survey tables with pandas (made-up data).

Fill in the TODOs, then run:  python reef_tables.py
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# 1. A Series: depth by site
depth = pd.Series({"S01": 4.5, "S02": 12.0, "S03": 6.0, "S04": 18.5, "S05": 9.0, "S06": 3.5}, name="depth_m")
# TODO: the depth of S04 by label, the first depth by position, and the sites deeper than 8 m

# 2. Alignment: two divers counted coral colonies by genus
diver_a = pd.Series({"Acropora": 14, "Porites": 9, "Pocillopora": 5})
diver_b = pd.Series({"Porites": 11, "Montipora": 4, "Acropora": 10})
# TODO: add them with +, then with .add(..., fill_value=0), and print both
both = total = pd.Series(dtype=float)
print("With +:", both.to_dict())
print("With add(fill_value=0):", total.to_dict())

# 3. Load the export. Look at the file first: comments start with #, fields are separated by semicolons,
# decimals use commas, and missing values are written n/a or -.
# TODO: the right read_csv options, with island as a category and fish_count as the nullable Int64
surveys = pd.read_csv("reef_surveys.csv")
print("Shape:", surveys.shape)
print("Types:", surveys.dtypes[["depth_m", "coral_pct", "fish_count", "island"]].astype(str).to_dict())
print("Missing:", surveys.isna().sum()[lambda s: s > 0].to_dict())

# 4. Dates written day.month.year
# TODO: convert the date column with pd.to_datetime and an explicit format
print("From", surveys["date"].min().date(), "to", surveys["date"].max().date())

# 5. A MultiIndex of site and date
# TODO: set_index(["site_id", "date"]) and sort_index(), then select site S03's coral cover
indexed = surveys
print("Index is unique:", indexed.index.is_unique)
print("S03 coral cover:", indexed.loc["S03", "coral_pct"].tolist())

# 6. Changing values safely. One coral cover of 340 is impossible.
surveys[surveys["coral_pct"] > 100]["coral_pct"] = np.nan    # chained assignment: what happens?
print("Max after chained assignment:", surveys["coral_pct"].max())
# TODO: blank the impossible value in one step with .loc
print("Max after .loc:", surveys["coral_pct"].max())
eastern = surveys[surveys["island"] == "Eastern Reef"].copy()
eastern["coral_pct"] = 0
print(f"Mean coral cover is still {surveys['coral_pct'].mean():.2f} after changing the copy")

# 7. A DataFrame from records, one dictionary per row
records = [{"site_id": "S07", "island": "Northern Atoll", "depth_m": 7.5},
           {"site_id": "S08", "island": "Western Lagoon", "depth_m": 11.0}]
new_sites = pd.DataFrame(records)
print("New sites:", new_sites.shape, new_sites.columns.tolist())

hints: pandas 3 warns with a ChainedAssignmentError and pandas 2 with a SettingWithCopyWarning; either way the original isn't changed.
Without decimal=',', a value such as 34,5 can't be read as a number, so the column stays text.
indexed.loc['S03', 'coral_pct'] selects every date for S03 from the first index level.

modules.title: Data Cleaning and Preparation
modules.summary: Find and handle missing data, sentinel values and impossible readings, fill gaps by group and over time, and transform messy text, units and categories into clean, typed columns you can trust.

lessons.title: Missing data: NaN, NA and sentinels
objectives: Recognise the ways missing data appears in pandas and in files
Measure how much is missing, and where
key_points: pandas represents missing values as NaN in float columns, NaT in datetime columns and <NA> in its nullable types (Int64, boolean, string); None in a column is treated as missing too.
NaN isn't equal to anything, itself included, so df['x'] == np.nan is always False; isna() and notna() are the reliable tests.
Files hide missing values as sentinels such as -999, 0, '-' or 'unknown'. Convert them with na_values= when reading, or replace({-999: np.nan}) afterwards, or they distort every statistic.
read_csv also treats strings such as NA, N/A, null and None as missing by default, so a category really called None can vanish; keep_default_na=False with your own na_values list prevents that.
df.isna().sum() counts the missing values per column, df.isna().mean() gives the share, and df[df.isna().any(axis=1)] shows the incomplete rows themselves.
Ask why a value is missing before fixing it: a failed sensor, a survey that never happened and a reading too high to record are different problems that need different treatments.

lessons.title: Dropping and filling: dropna, fillna and interpolate
objectives: Drop rows or columns with missing values deliberately
Fill gaps with constants, group statistics, neighbours or interpolation
key_points: dropna() drops every row with a missing value; how='all' drops only empty rows, subset=['coral_pct'] looks only at the columns that matter, thresh=n keeps rows with at least n values, and axis=1 drops columns instead.
fillna(value) fills with one value, or with a dictionary of values per column, and returns a new object, so assign the result: df['visibility_m'] = df['visibility_m'].fillna(0).

In ordered data, ffill() and bfill() copy the neighbouring value and interpolate() estimates from the values on both sides; limit=n caps how many missing values in a row are filled, though in a longer gap it still fills the first n.
Fill by group with each group's own statistic: df['temp'].fillna(df.groupby('site')['temp'].transform('median')) fills each site's gaps with that site's median rather than the overall one.
Every fill invents data, so record it: a flag such as df['temp_imputed'] = df['temp'].isna(), set before filling, lets later analyses tell measured values from estimates.

lessons.title: Transforming values: text, units and categories
objectives: Standardise labels and extract numbers and units from text
Convert columns to the right numeric and categorical types
key_points: The .str accessor applies string methods to a whole column: str.strip(), str.upper(), str.contains() and str.replace(r'[^A-Z0-9]', '', regex=True), which removes every character that isn't a capital letter or a digit.
str.extract(r'(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*(m|cm)?') pulls a regular expression's groups out into columns, such as a number and its unit, so that values in mixed units can be converted.
map(dictionary) replaces each value with its match and turns everything unmatched into NaN, which exposes labels you forgot; replace(dictionary) changes only the matches and leaves the rest alone.
pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce') turns unreadable text into NaN; count the NaN before and after, because a value a person could read, such as 1,250, may have been lost.

pd.CategoricalDtype(['none', 'low', 'moderate', 'severe'], ordered=True) stores labels once and gives them an order, so sorting and comparisons such as >= 'moderate' follow severity, not the alphabet.
pd.cut(values, bins) puts numbers into labelled ranges, and pd.qcut(values, q=4) into groups of equal size, such as quartiles.

lessons.title: Duplicates, impossible values and validation
objectives: Find exact and key-based duplicates and decide which to keep
Write checks that stop bad data from reaching an analysis
key_points: duplicated() flags rows that repeat an earlier row; subset=['survey_id'] compares only the key, and keep=False marks every copy, so you can inspect them all before choosing which to keep.

Normalise keys before looking for duplicates: 's01', 'S01 ' and 'S-01' are the same site only once they've been cleaned to 'S01'. Copies that share a key but disagree on other values need a decision, not an automatic drop.

Range checks catch impossible values: df['coral_pct'].between(0, 100) is False for a cover of 640%, probably 64.0 typed without its decimal point. Decide whether to correct, blank or drop it, and record the decision.
clip(lower, upper) caps values at limits, which suits an instrument with a known range, but it hides errors when it's used on values that are simply wrong.
Turn the rules into checks that fail loudly: assert df['survey_id'].is_unique and assert df['coral_pct'].between(0, 100).all() stop a pipeline before bad data spreads.
Chain cleaning steps as small functions with pipe() and assign(), as in raw.pipe(clean_codes).pipe(drop_impossible), so that each step can be read and tested on its own.

"""Clean a messy reef monitoring export and a temperature logger's readings with pandas (made-up data).

Fill in the TODOs, then run:  python clean_reef.py
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

naive = pd.read_csv("reef_raw.csv")
print("Bleaching values read as missing by default:", int(naive["bleaching"].isna().sum()))
# TODO: read the file again so that only blank cells and n/a count as missing (keep_default_na=False, na_values=...)
raw = naive.copy()
print("Rows:", len(raw), "bleaching missing:", int(raw["bleaching"].isna().sum()))

# 1. Sentinels: the water temperature uses -999 for "no reading"
print("Missing temperatures as loaded:", int(raw["water_temp_c"].isna().sum()))
# TODO: replace -999 with NaN in water_temp_c
print("Missing temperatures after replacing -999:", int(raw["water_temp_c"].isna().sum()))

# 2. Site codes are typed several ways (s01, S-01, " S02"): make them all like S01
print("Site spellings:", raw["site"].nunique())
# TODO: strip, upper case, then remove anything that isn't a letter or digit with str.replace and a regex
print("Sites after cleaning:", sorted(raw["site"].unique()))

# 3. Duplicates: some surveys were exported twice
print("Exact duplicates now:", int(raw.duplicated().sum()))
print("Rows sharing a survey_id:", int(raw.duplicated(subset="survey_id", keep=False).sum()))
shared = raw[raw.duplicated(subset="survey_id", keep=False)].drop_duplicates()
print("Survey ids whose copies disagree:", sorted(shared.loc[shared.duplicated("survey_id", keep=False), "survey_id"].unique()))
# TODO: drop the duplicates, keeping the first of each survey_id
surveys = raw.copy()
print("Surveys after removing duplicates:", len(surveys))

# 4. Impossible coral cover: outside 0 to 100 percent
bad = ~surveys["coral_pct"].between(0, 100) & surveys["coral_pct"].notna()
print("Impossible coral cover values:", surveys.loc[bad, "coral_pct"].tolist())
# TODO: set them to NaN with .loc

# 5. Visibility: "12 m", "8m", "15" or "900 cm": extract the number and the unit, and convert to metres
# TODO: str.extract with two groups, then divide the cm values by 100
surveys["visibility_m"] = np.nan
print(f"Visibility: mean {surveys['visibility_m'].mean():.1f} m, max {surveys['visibility_m'].max():.0f} m, "
      f"missing {int(surveys['visibility_m'].isna().sum())}")

# 6. Bleaching: one spelling per level, then an ordered category
levels = ["none", "low", "moderate", "severe"]
# TODO: strip and lower-case, then convert to pd.CategoricalDtype(levels, ordered=True)
print("Bleaching:", surveys["bleaching"].value_counts(sort=False).to_dict())
print("Moderate or worse:", int((surveys["bleaching"] >= "moderate").sum()))

# 7. Fill missing temperatures with each site's median, and flag them
# TODO: the flag first, then fillna with groupby("site")["water_temp_c"].transform("median")
surveys["temp_imputed"] = False
print("Temperatures filled:", int(surveys["temp_imputed"].sum()),
      "still missing:", int(surveys["water_temp_c"].isna().sum()))

# 8. Coral cover is the key measurement: drop the surveys without it, then check the rules
# TODO: dropna with subset
clean = surveys
assert clean["survey_id"].is_unique
assert clean["coral_pct"].between(0, 100).all()
print("Clean surveys:", len(clean), f"mean coral cover {clean['coral_pct'].mean():.1f}%")

# 9. The logger: daily temperatures with gaps
logger = pd.read_csv("logger.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")
print("Logger gaps:", int(logger["temp_c"].isna().sum()))
# TODO: interpolate only gaps of up to 2 days (limit=2 and limit_area="inside"), and count what's left
filled = logger["temp_c"]
print("Still missing after interpolating:", int(filled.isna().sum()))
print("Filled value on 2024-03-06:", round(filled.loc["2024-03-06"], 2))

modules.title: Data Wrangling: Join, Combine, and Reshape
modules.summary: Combine tables with merges you validate and audit, stack and patch data with concat and combine_first, match readings in time with merge_asof, and reshape between long and wide with melt, pivot, stack and unstack.

lessons.title: Merging on keys: relationships and validation
objectives: Merge DataFrames on one or more keys with the right type of join
Validate a merge's relationship and audit the rows that didn't match
key_points: pd.merge(left, right, on='soum_id', how=...) joins rows with matching keys: 'inner' keeps the matches only, 'left' every left row, 'right' every right row and 'outer' all of them, with NaN where one side has no match.
Keys with different names use left_on= and right_on=, several keys are passed as a list, and suffixes=('_2023', '_2024') renames columns that appear in both tables.

State the relationship you expect: validate='many_to_one' raises a MergeError if the right table repeats a key, which would otherwise duplicate left rows without any warning; 'one_to_one' and 'one_to_many' work the same way.
indicator=True adds a _merge column saying both, left_only or right_only for each row, which shows exactly which keys failed to match and explains any change in the number of rows.

Most failed matches come from keys that look alike but aren't, such as 'c07' and 'C07' or a trailing space, or from different types, such as 7 and '7'. Clean and type the keys first, and compare the row counts before and after.

lessons.title: Concatenating, joining on the index and patching gaps
objectives: Stack tables with concat and record where each row came from
Join on the index, patch gaps from a second source and match readings by time
key_points: pd.concat([a, b]) stacks tables vertically, matching columns by name and filling missing ones with NaN; ignore_index=True numbers the rows afresh, and keys=[2023, 2024] labels each part with an outer index level.
pd.concat(axis=1) puts tables side by side, aligned on the index, and df.join(other) joins on the index as well, keeping every row of df by default.
Two exports that overlap produce repeated rows when stacked, and concat keeps them without a warning; check with duplicated(subset=keys) straight after stacking.
a.combine_first(b) fills a's missing values with b's values for the same labels, which suits patching one source with a second, less trusted one.

pd.merge_asof(visits, passes, on='date', by='soum_id', direction='backward', tolerance=pd.Timedelta('10D')) matches each visit with the latest earlier pass over the same soum, within 10 days; both tables must be sorted by the date column.

lessons.title: Reshaping: melt, pivot, stack and unstack
objectives: Reshape data between wide and long forms
Move index levels between the rows and the columns
key_points: Long, or tidy, data has one row per observation and one column per variable, such as soum, year, species and head; wide data spreads one variable across columns, such as a column for each species.
melt(id_vars=['soum_id', 'year'], var_name='species', value_name='head') turns wide columns into long rows, the form that groupby, merges and most plotting libraries expect.

pivot(index='soum_id', columns='species', values='head') turns long into wide, but raises ValueError (Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape) when an index and column pair appears twice; pivot_table() aggregates the repeats instead.
stack() moves the innermost column level into the row index and unstack() moves an index level into the columns, as in df.groupby(['aimag', 'year'])['units'].sum().unstack('year').
explode() gives each item of a list in a cell its own row, which turns a column such as 'sheep;goat' into long data after str.split(';').

modules.title: Data Aggregation and Group Operations
modules.summary: Master split-apply-combine with groupby: aggregate with built-in, named and custom functions, transform values within groups, filter whole groups, and summarise in two dimensions with pivot tables and crosstabs.

lessons.title: Split-apply-combine with groupby
objectives: Explain split-apply-combine and group by one or several keys
Control how keys, missing values and categories appear in the result
key_points: df.groupby(keys) splits the rows into groups that share key values, applies a calculation to each and combines the results into one object; nothing is computed until you call an aggregation or another method.
Keys can be column names, a list of columns, a Series or array of the same length, or a function of the index; they become the result's index, unless as_index=False keeps them as columns.
size() counts every row in each group, while count() counts each column's non-missing values, so the two differ when values are missing.

Rows whose key is NaN are left out unless dropna=False. With categorical keys, observed=True, the default in pandas 3, shows only the categories that occur; pandas 2 also listed empty ones by default.
for name, group in df.groupby('aimag'): loops over (key, DataFrame) pairs, which is useful for looking at one group, but the aggregation methods are much faster than a loop.

lessons.title: Aggregation: built-in, named and custom
objectives: Compute several summaries per group in one step with named aggregation
Aggregate time series by period and combine it with other keys
key_points: Built-in aggregations such as mean, median, sum, min, max, std, nunique, first and last run in fast compiled code: df.groupby('soum_id')['biomass_g_m2'].mean().
Named aggregation names each result column: agg(visits=('plot_id', 'size'), plots=('plot_id', 'nunique'), mean_biomass=('biomass_g_m2', 'mean')).
A custom function receives each group's values as a Series, as in ('biomass_g_m2', lambda s: s.quantile(0.9)); it runs in Python once per group, so use a built-in name whenever one exists.
A weighted mean needs two columns, so compute the pieces per group, the sum of weight times value and the sum of the weights, then divide; averaging group averages gives small groups too much weight.

Time series aggregate by period with resample('MS', on='date') or groupby(pd.Grouper(key='date', freq='MS')), which can be combined with other keys such as aimag; 'MS' means calendar months, labelled by their first day.

lessons.title: transform, filter and apply
objectives: Add group statistics back to every row with transform
Keep or drop whole groups with filter, and know when apply is needed
key_points: transform returns a result the same length as its input, aligned with the original rows: df.groupby('soum_id')['biomass_g_m2'].transform('mean') puts each soum's mean on each of its rows.
That makes within-group comparisons one line each: the deviation from the group mean, a z-score within the group, each row's share of its group's total, or a gap filled with the group's median.
filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 8) keeps or drops whole groups by a condition on the group, such as removing soums with too few visits to trust their averages.
Ranks and counters work within groups without loops: groupby(...).rank(ascending=False) ranks rows inside each group, cumcount() numbers them, and shift() and cumsum() stay within each group.
apply() runs any function on each group's DataFrame, which makes it the most flexible option and also the slowest; use it when agg, transform and filter can't express the calculation.

lessons.title: Pivot tables and crosstabs
objectives: Summarise data in two dimensions with pivot_table and crosstab
Add totals and turn counts into proportions
key_points: pivot_table(index='aimag', columns='year', values='biomass_g_m2', aggfunc='mean') puts one key down the rows and another across the columns and aggregates every combination.
margins=True adds an All row and column computed from the underlying rows, so in a table of means the margins are overall means, not means of the means; fill_value replaces empty combinations.
aggfunc can be a list, such as ['mean', 'count'], giving a column level for each function, which shows how many rows lie behind each value.

pd.crosstab(df['aimag'], df['grazing']) counts the combinations of two categories; normalize='index' turns each row into proportions, normalize='columns' each column and normalize='all' the whole table.
A pivot table is a groupby on two keys followed by unstack; choose whichever reads more clearly, and remember that tables people read are wide, while data you analyse stays long.

plots["anomaly"] = plots["z_in_aimag"] = 0.0

project.title: Real-World Dataset Cleaning Capstone: an air-quality network
project.brief: A city's air-quality network (made-up data) has six stations measuring PM2.5, PM10 and NO2 every day. You have the first quarter of 2025 in two overlapping exports (readings_part1.csv and readings_part2.csv), the station list (stations.csv) and the daily weather (weather.csv). They're messy: station codes are typed several ways (aq01, AQ-01, ' AQ02'), dates are written 2025-01-14 or 14/01/2025, -999 means no reading, <5 means below the detection limit, a few rows are in mg/m3 instead of µg/m3, some station-days are absent and the overlap repeats rows. Build a pandas pipeline that turns them into one clean table with one row per station and day, then answer the city's questions. The rules: normalise the codes; parse each date format explicitly rather than relying on dayfirst; remove duplicates; treat -999 as missing and <5 as 2.5, half the limit; convert mg/m3 to µg/m3; validate the merges with the stations and the weather; reindex to every station and day from 1 January to 31 March; and fill gaps with interpolate(limit=2, limit_area='inside') within each station, flagging every filled value. Then report the mean PM2.5 by station and month, the days over the city's alert level of 25 µg/m3 (made up for this project) by station, the differences between roadside, industrial and background sites, and calm days (wind under 2 m/s) against windy ones. Check yourself: 553 rows read, 29 exact duplicates, 6 values below the detection limit, 9 rows in mg/m3, 16 of the 540 station-days absent, 1 PM2.5 value still missing after interpolation, and a January mean of 28.5 µg/m3 at AQ01.
deliverables: A notebook or script that rebuilds the clean table from the four raw files from a fresh start, as small functions chained with pipe()
clean_readings.csv: 540 rows, one per station and day, with each station's details, the weather and a flag for every filled value
A cleaning log: each problem, how many rows it affected, and what was done about it
Validation checks (asserts) for the rules: unique station-days, no sentinels left, values in µg/m3 within sensible ranges, and every merge validated
Summary tables: mean PM2.5 by station and month (a pivot table), days over 25 µg/m3 by station, means by site type, and calm against windy days
A short write-up of what the data shows, and how the cleaning decisions and filled values could affect it
Optionally, the same pipeline run on a messy open dataset you choose, with a supplementary table merged in

rubric.name: Cleaning
rubric.description: Codes, dates, sentinels, detection limits, units, duplicates and gaps are handled as the rules say, and the self-check numbers match.

rubric.name: Combining and reshaping
rubric.description: The exports are stacked, every merge is validated and audited with no silent loss or duplication of rows, and the station-by-day grid is built with reindex.

rubric.name: Aggregation
rubric.description: groupby, transform, pivot tables and crosstabs answer each question correctly and clearly.

rubric.name: Code quality and reproducibility
rubric.description: Small functions in a pipe() chain, vectorised operations rather than loops, clear names, and code that runs from top to bottom on a fresh start.

rubric.name: Validation and write-up
rubric.description: Asserts that would catch each problem if it came back, a complete cleaning log, and a write-up that is honest about filled and missing values.

project.submit: Paste your pipeline code, the output of your checks and summary tables, the first ten rows of clean_readings.csv, your cleaning log and your write-up.
